newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Vietnam economy buoyant, but government worried.
newsitem.headline: Vietnam economy buoyant, but government worried.

text.p: Vietnam released a host of statistics on Monday showing double-digit growth in industrial output and a narrowing trade deficit, but a government report expressed concern about signs of economic slowdown.
The General Statistics Office said industrial production rose by 13.8 percent in the first four months of this year from the same period of 1996.
The country's trade deficit, a growing cause for concern last year as imports were sucked in faster than goods could be sold abroad, was 30.2 percent lower than a year earlier at $962 million.
But in spite of the apparently glowing picture that those figures painted, a Government Office report obtained by Reuters revealed growing concern in official circles about economic stagnation.
The report pointed to news that consumer prices had dropped for the second month in row, taking the year-on-year inflation rate to 1.6 percent -- its lowest in over a decade.
"Deflation has appeared earlier than in previous years," the report said. "This situation contains many factors which will cause stagnation for production and trade in the coming months."
It said economic weaknesses had come to light in the past four months, with some domestic goods struggling to compete against foreign imports and economic growth in general slowing down.
The report added that foreign direct investment (FDI), which has been one of the strongest motors in Vietnam's six-year-old economic explosion, had fallen.
Although the number of FDI projects increased by 25 percent in the first 3-1/2 months of this year compared with the same period of last year, the value of those projects was down 13 percent.
The report also highlighted a slowdown in the disbursement of official development aid (ODA), blaming procedural hold-ups and complications.
ODA disbursement in the first quarter was put at $250 million, which met just 16 percent of the government's annual plan.

The Government Office also pointed to figures showing that credit had grown by just four percent since the beginning of this year, saying that was too low for an economy which was crying out for capital.
